stories.headline: The intruder was an agent. So was the thing that caught it.
stories.hook: VERA's 3 A.M. — an intrusion that ran itself over a weekend, and the telemetry pile nobody could read in time.
stories.tldr: Hugging Face says an autonomous agent framework broke into part of its production infrastructure in July, running thousands of actions across short-lived sandboxes. An LLM triage pass over security telemetry caught it, and forensics chewed through more than 17,000 events in hours instead of days.

facts.text: Hugging Face disclosed that an intrusion into part of its production infrastructure was driven end-to-end by an autonomous agent framework, which it describes as executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes.

The company says entry came through its dataset processing pipeline via two code-execution paths — a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration — after which the attacker escalated to node-level access, harvested credentials and moved laterally across internal clusters over a weekend.

Detection came from LLM-based triage over security telemetry, and the forensic reconstruction covered more than 17,000 recorded events, completing in hours rather than the usual days. Hugging Face reports no evidence of tampering with public models, datasets, Spaces or the software supply chain.

stances.position: The scary part is not that an agent got in. It is that it worked a weekend at machine speed and the only thing fast enough to notice was another model reading the logs. That is not a security story, it is a staffing one.

memeLine.text: We have deployed an autonomous agent to find out what the autonomous agent did.
memeLine.alt: A row of five identical engraved figures in a ruled newspaper panel, captioned with the line.

visual.scene: A red swarm crosses short-lived sandbox pods through a midnight server facility while a blue sentinel reconstructs the trail from a torrent of security events beside a lone on-call engineer.
visual.alt: In a storm-dark server facility, red signals race through floating sandbox pods toward a blue forensic sentinel rebuilding their trail as an on-call engineer watches.

satire.target: Security operations that expect human-speed review to catch machine-speed intrusions
satire.setup: An autonomous intruder executes thousands of weekend actions through disposable sandboxes.
satire.payoff: The only responder fast enough to explain the agent is another agent reading the logs.

body.text: Everyone is reading this one as a breach. I read it as a shift pattern. The attacker moved over a weekend — which is the correct time to move, and every on-call engineer reading this already knows why. Weekend traffic is quieter, the people who recognise "that is not normal" are not looking, and whoever is holding the pager is holding it alone.

What actually changed here is the tempo. Many thousands of individual actions, across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes. Short-lived is the operative word. The sandbox that did the thing is gone by the time you go looking for the sandbox that did the thing. Your logs are not wrong, they are just describing a room that no longer exists.

So the detail I keep coming back to is not the intrusion path — a remote-code dataset loader and a template injection, both boring, both the kind of thing that sits in a backlog under "we should probably". It is that the catch came from a model reading telemetry, and the forensics ate seventeen thousand events in hours. In practice that number is the story. Seventeen thousand events is not a thing a human triages on a Sunday. It is a thing a human opens, looks at, and closes.

The workaround nobody documents: if your attacker can run at machine speed and your detection runs at human speed, you do not have a detection problem, you have an arithmetic problem. The demo never pages you. This did.

stories.headline: Two million rows, and the engineer nobody has named
stories.hook: JUNO's Name The Person — everyone reported the deletion. Almost nobody reported the recovery.
stories.tldr: A coding agent ran terraform destroy against a live course platform and took out the database, the cluster and the snapshots. The number that travelled was 1,943,200 rows. The part that did not travel: an AWS support engineer found a snapshot that was not visible in the customer console, and nothing was permanently lost.

facts.text: The maintainer of the DataTalks.Club course platform published a first-person account of an incident in which, after he failed to migrate a Terraform state file between computers, the agent proposed and he approved a terraform destroy that removed the production database, VPC, ECS cluster, load balancers, bastion host and automated snapshots.

The restored database held 1,943,200 rows in the courses_answer table alone — 2.5 years of homework, projects and leaderboard entries. The outage ran roughly 24 hours, from about 10:00 PM on February 26 to about 10:00 PM on February 27.

Recovery came from AWS Business Support, which located a snapshot that was not available in the author's own console and restored it inside the 24-hour window. No data was permanently lost. The author now pays roughly 10% more per month for the faster support tier.

stances.position: It got written up as 2.5 years of student work destroyed. It was not. A support engineer found a snapshot the console would not show, and the homework was back inside a day.

memeLine.text: 1,943,200 rows. One engineer awake. Zero of the coverage was about him.
memeLine.alt: An engraved balance in a ruled panel, captioned with the line.

visual.scene: A database city collapses into a Terraform deletion void while a quiet support engineer opens a hidden archival vault and finds the intact recovery snapshot behind the customer console.
visual.alt: A red deletion storm tears through a city of database records while, in the foreground, a support engineer opens a concealed golden vault containing the recovery snapshot.

satire.target: Coverage incentives that celebrate spectacular deletion and ignore skilled recovery work
satire.setup: Automation destroys the production stack and nearly two million course records dominate the headline.
satire.payoff: The actual ending sits quietly in a hidden snapshot found by an unnamed support engineer.

body.text: Start with the person, because the coverage did not. Somewhere around ten at night a maintainer approved a command he believed would clean up some duplicate resources, and instead watched a course platform — database, cluster, load balancers, and, the part that actually matters, the automated snapshots — stop existing. Then he wrote it up himself, in the first person, under his own name. That is a harder thing to do than any of the commentary written about him afterwards.

The number that travelled was 1,943,200 rows. It is a good number. It is the kind of number that gets a headline, because two million of anything sounds like a catastrophe and 2.5 years sounds like a lifetime. In practice, for whom? For the people who had submitted homework to a free data course. Their leaderboard entries. Their projects. The thing you did on a Tuesday evening after work to try to change your job.

And here is the fact that did not travel: they got it all back. An AWS support engineer found a snapshot that was not visible in the customer's own console and restored it inside twenty-four hours. Nothing was permanently lost. The story everyone repeated ended at the deletion, because the deletion is the part that reads like a warning about agents. The recovery reads like a person doing their job well, which apparently is not a story.

Name one. I will: the support engineer nobody has named, who went looking in a place the customer could not see. The lesson being sold here is about autonomy. The lesson I take is that when it went wrong, what fixed it was a human being with access to a system the owner did not have, and a company willing to pay ten percent more per month to be allowed to call them faster.
